articles.title: KURA Announces Three-Hour Outer Ring Road Closure This Saturday
articles.desc: Nairobi motorists will face disruption on Outer Ring Road this Saturday as KURA removes an overhead gantry near Airport North Road.
articles.content:
Nairobi motorists using Outer Ring Road have been advised to plan their journeys ahead of a scheduled three-hour traffic disruption this Saturday, September 5, 2026.

The Kenya Urban Roads Authority (KURA) announced on Wednesday, September 2, that part of the busy Nairobi road will be affected between 12pm and 3pm to allow for the removal of an overhead gantry near the Airport North Road junction.

According to the traffic management plan, the operation will take place in three stages. From 12pm to 1pm, machinery will be moved into position while traffic continues at reduced speed.

The affected section will then face a full closure between 1pm and 2pm as crews remove the gantry. Traffic is expected to resume from 2pm to 3pm, although motorists may still experience reduced speeds as equipment is removed and the work area is cleared.

KURA has urged motorists to plan their travel in advance and cooperate with traffic police officers and marshals who will be deployed during the operation.

The Nairobi Outer Ring Road closure is likely to affect motorists travelling through the eastern parts of the city, particularly those connecting through the Airport North Road area.

Outer Ring Road is an important transport corridor linking major routes and serving thousands of commuters and public service vehicles daily. Any temporary closure along the route can therefore cause delays, especially during busy weekend travel periods.

Motorists travelling through the area may need to consider alternative routes depending on their destination. Routes around Mombasa Road, Airport South Road and Airport North Road have been identified in traffic advisories as options for avoiding the affected section.

For Nairobi residents, the latest KURA traffic advisory is important because the disruption has been announced several days before the planned works, giving motorists, matatu operators and businesses time to adjust their travel plans.

Drivers planning to use Outer Ring Road on Saturday afternoon are advised to allow extra travel time, avoid the affected section during the full closure where possible and follow instructions issued by traffic officers at the site.

The works are scheduled to end at 3pm on Saturday, after which normal traffic flow is expected to resume.

articles.title: FKF Meets Clubs as 2026/27 League Start Remains Uncertain
articles.desc: FKF held talks with clubs on September 2 as Kenya's 2026/27 top-flight season remains affected by a dispute over league rules.
articles.content:
Football Kenya Federation (FKF) held a fresh meeting with top-flight clubs on Wednesday, September 2, as uncertainty continued to surround the start of the 2026/27 Kenyan Premier League season.

The meeting brought together representatives of league clubs and FKF officials as the federation seeks to address key issues affecting preparations for the new campaign. FKF Chief Executive Officer Dennis Gicheru and Leagues and Competitions Head Frank Ogolla were reported to have led the discussions.

The talks came after the start of the new Kenyan Premier League season was disrupted by a legal dispute over the regulations governing promotion and relegation.

FKF had initially planned for the new season to begin in August, but the opening round of fixtures was postponed as the federation, clubs and other stakeholders continued consultations.

The dispute has centred on which FKF rules should govern the 2026/27 season and how promotion and relegation should be handled.

A High Court clarification has indicated that FKF can run its national leagues under the 2019 FKF Rules and Regulations, which remain unaffected by the current petition. The 2019 rules include a mandatory promotion and relegation playoff, an issue that has been central to the ongoing disagreement.

FKF President Hussein Mohammed has also acknowledged the need for further consultations with clubs before a clear way forward is agreed.

The federation's latest meeting is therefore significant for Kenyan football because clubs, players and supporters are still waiting for confirmation of when the 2026/27 campaign will officially begin.

The uncertainty has also affected clubs' preparations. Teams normally use the period before the start of a new season to finalise squads, prepare match strategies and plan their competitive schedules. With the league programme disrupted, clubs are instead waiting for clarity on the regulations and the new kick-off arrangements.

For football fans, the situation means another delay in the return of regular top-flight action involving clubs such as Gor Mahia, AFC Leopards, Tusker and Kenya Police.

Wednesday's talks represent a fresh attempt to bring stakeholders together, but FKF is yet to confirm whether the discussions will immediately lead to a new start date for the league.

The next decisions by the federation and the outcome of the legal process will be closely watched as Kenyan football seeks a resolution and a stable start to the 2026/27 season.

articles.title: Kenya Investors Question Sh5 Billion SEZ Investment Threshold
articles.desc: Investors question Kenya's Sh5 billion SEZ threshold, warning it could lock smaller businesses out of long-term licences.
articles.content:
Investors are raising concerns over Kenya's Sh5 billion Special Economic Zones (SEZ) investment threshold, with questions emerging over whether the requirement could make it harder for smaller businesses to access long-term operating licences.

The concerns have renewed attention on Kenya's Special Economic Zones framework, which is designed to attract investment, expand manufacturing and support job creation through designated areas offering a favourable environment for businesses.

Under changes to the SEZ framework, major investments meeting the Sh5 billion threshold can qualify for a special licence with a longer operating period. The provision was intended to give large, capital-intensive projects greater certainty while encouraging significant investments in Kenya.

However, some investors are now questioning whether the high Kenya SEZ investment threshold could create a gap between large corporations and smaller businesses with viable projects but less capital.

The issue is particularly important for local and regional investors seeking opportunities in manufacturing, agro-processing, technology and other sectors targeted under Kenya's industrialisation agenda.

Supporters of the threshold argue that large-scale projects often require substantial capital and longer investment periods before generating returns. They say offering long-term certainty could help Kenya compete for major investments and strengthen the country's position as a regional business hub.

Parliamentary discussions around the Special Economic Zones reforms also indicated that the investment threshold could be reviewed over time, depending on economic conditions and changes in the value of the shilling.

President William Ruto assented to the Special Economic Zones (Amendment) legislation in May 2026 as part of broader efforts to strengthen Kenya's investment environment and widen the range of sectors operating within SEZs.

The reforms are expected to support activities including manufacturing, agro-processing, mining, technology and other strategic industries.

For ordinary Kenyans, the debate over SEZ investment in Kenya goes beyond licensing rules. Major investments can create jobs, increase demand for local suppliers and contribute to economic growth. At the same time, policymakers face pressure to ensure that smaller Kenyan businesses are not left behind as the country seeks large-scale foreign and domestic investment.

The latest concerns over the Sh5 billion threshold could therefore reopen debate on how Kenya balances attracting major investors with creating space for smaller businesses to participate in the country's industrial growth.

As the SEZ reforms continue to take effect, investors and policymakers will be watching closely to see whether the investment requirement remains unchanged or is reviewed to reflect Kenya's changing economic environment.

articles.title: Government Releases KSh850 Million Cash Support for Vulnerable Families
articles.desc: The government has released KSh850.7 million to support more than 425,000 households caring for orphans and vulnerable children.
articles.content:
The government has released more than KSh850 million to support households enrolled in the Cash Transfer for Orphans and Vulnerable Children programme under the Inua Jamii social protection initiative.

Gender, Culture and Children Services Cabinet Secretary Hanna Wendot Cheptumo announced the latest disbursement on Wednesday, saying a total of KSh850,696,000 had been allocated to 425,348 beneficiary households across the country.

Under the payment cycle, each eligible household is set to receive KSh2,000 for the July 2026 payment.

The funds are intended to support families caring for orphans and vulnerable children, helping them meet basic household needs and provide care for children living in vulnerable circumstances.

According to the announcement, payments began on September 1 through the government's contracted Payment Service Provider.

The latest release provides fresh support to families who depend on social protection programmes to help meet everyday expenses.

For many vulnerable households, cash assistance can help with essential needs such as food, clothing and other basic requirements, particularly at a time when many families continue to face pressure from the cost of living.

The Cash Transfer for Orphans and Vulnerable Children programme is implemented through the State Department for Children Services as part of the wider Inua Jamii initiative.

Inua Jamii is among the government's key social protection programmes and is designed to provide financial assistance to eligible vulnerable groups and households.

The latest disbursement focuses specifically on households caring for orphans and vulnerable children, with more than 425,000 households included in the current payment cycle.

Beneficiaries have also been urged to follow the established payment procedures when accessing their funds and remain alert to fraudsters who may attempt to take advantage of the disbursement.

The announcement is likely to bring relief to families awaiting the payment, particularly those who rely on the support to supplement their household income.

As payments continue, attention will now turn to ensuring that eligible beneficiaries receive their funds smoothly and without unnecessary delays.

The latest release also highlights the continued role of cash transfer programmes in supporting vulnerable families and cushioning households facing financial challenges across Kenya.

articles.title: Court Told Key Nairobi CCTV Cameras Were Offline During Rex Masai Shooting
articles.desc: An inquest has heard that key Nairobi CBD CCTV cameras were offline during the 2024 shooting of protester Rex Masai.
articles.content:
Key police CCTV cameras in Nairobi's Central Business District were offline when protester Rex Masai was fatally shot during the June 2024 anti-Finance Bill demonstrations, a court has heard.

The fresh details emerged on Tuesday during the ongoing inquest into Masai's death, where Chief Inspector Andrew Limo, a technical officer attached to the National Police Service CCTV command centre, testified about the state of the surveillance network.

Limo told the court that cameras detectives wanted to rely on for footage were not operational at the time of the shooting.

Among them was a camera along Mama Ngina Street, an area linked to the events surrounding the demonstrations in Nairobi's CBD.

The court heard that a faulty fibre cable had affected parts of the CCTV network, leaving investigators without some of the recordings they had sought after the shooting.

The testimony has raised fresh questions about the reliability of surveillance systems in one of Nairobi's busiest areas.

CCTV footage can play an important role in investigations by helping authorities reconstruct events, identify people and establish timelines.

However, Limo told the court that the relevant cameras were offline when investigators sought footage connected to the June 20, 2024 demonstrations.

He was also questioned about whether the cameras around Mama Ngina Street had since been restored.

According to his testimony, the cameras remained offline.

The issue is significant for Nairobi because the CBD is a major centre for business, transport and public activity, where surveillance infrastructure can play an important role in security and investigations.

During the hearing, questions were raised about how investigators would handle a serious incident in an area where surveillance cameras were unavailable.

Limo told the court that police investigations do not rely entirely on CCTV footage and can use other sources of evidence.

The testimony does not determine responsibility for Masai's death, which remains the subject of the ongoing inquest. Instead, it adds fresh information about the availability of surveillance footage during the demonstrations.

The hearing was adjourned and is expected to continue as the court examines further evidence connected to the case.

For Nairobi residents, the latest testimony also brings renewed attention to the condition and maintenance of security infrastructure in the city centre.

articles.title: Kenya Airways Acting CEO George Kamal Resigns
articles.desc: Kenya Airways Acting CEO George Kamal has resigned, with Habil Waswani set to take over in an acting capacity from September 15.
articles.content:
Kenya Airways is facing another leadership transition after Acting Group Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer Capt. George Kamal resigned from the national carrier for personal reasons.

The airline announced the development on Tuesday, saying Kamal will remain in office during a 30-day transition period before formally leaving Kenya Airways on September 30, 2026.

Kamal has served as Acting Group Managing Director and CEO since December 16, 2025, after previously working as the airline's Chief Operating Officer.

During his time in executive leadership, Kenya Airways credited him with helping stabilise operations and supporting the implementation of its turnaround strategy.

The Board has appointed Habil Waswani, the airline's Company Secretary and Director of Legal Services and Regulatory Compliance, as the next Acting Group Managing Director and CEO.

Waswani is expected to assume the acting role on September 15 as the airline begins another phase of its leadership transition.

Kenya Airways has also started the process of recruiting a substantive Group Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer.

The leadership change comes at an important time for the national carrier as it continues efforts to strengthen its operations and manage financial and operational challenges.

For travellers and the wider business community, leadership stability at Kenya Airways remains important because the airline plays a major role in connecting Kenya with regional and international markets.

A change at the top does not immediately mean changes to scheduled flights or passenger services. However, the incoming leadership will play an important role in guiding the airline's operations and longer-term strategy.

Waswani brings experience from his work in legal, regulatory and corporate matters at Kenya Airways, where he has served for more than five years.

Attention will now turn to the transition process and the Board's search for a permanent CEO.

For Kenya Airways, the immediate task will be ensuring continuity during the handover while maintaining progress on its turnaround plans and day-to-day operations.

The Board's eventual choice of a substantive CEO will also be closely watched as the national carrier seeks to navigate its next chapter.

articles.title: Omanyala Ends 2026 Season Early After Heel Injury
articles.desc: Ferdinand Omanyala has ended his 2026 season after a stress fracture ruled him out of the Diamond League Final and Ultimate Championship.
articles.content:
Kenyan sprint star Ferdinand Omanyala has brought his 2026 season to an early end after suffering a stress fracture in the heel bone of his left foot.

The African 100m record holder confirmed the setback on Tuesday, saying the injury will prevent him from competing in his final two races of the season.

Omanyala will now miss the Diamond League Final in Brussels as well as the inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championship, bringing an unexpected end to a campaign that had produced several encouraging performances.

The sprinter said the injury was sustained two weeks before the Commonwealth Games and continued to affect his preparations and performances.

Despite the disappointing conclusion, Omanyala reflected positively on his 2026 campaign.

He recorded five consecutive sub-10-second performances during the season and finished third in the Diamond League standings, earning direct qualification for the Ultimate Championship.

His strong performances had raised hopes of another major breakthrough for Kenyan sprinting, particularly ahead of the Diamond League Final, where he had qualified to compete against some of the world's leading 100m runners.

The injury, however, means those plans have now been put on hold as the focus shifts from competition to recovery.

For Kenyan athletics fans, the news is a major setback because Omanyala remains one of the country's most recognisable track athletes and a key figure in Kenya's growing sprinting profile.

His absence from the season-ending events will also deny him the opportunity to build on the consistency he showed earlier in the year.

Still, the season leaves positives for the 100m star. His run of five consecutive sub-10-second performances underlined his ability to compete at the highest level, while his Diamond League ranking showed he remained among the leading sprinters on the circuit.

Omanyala will now turn his attention towards recovery and rehabilitation as he prepares for the next stage of his athletics career.

While his 2026 campaign has ended earlier than expected, his performances during the season leave Kenyan fans with reasons to remain hopeful about his return to the track.

articles.title: Principals Warn Funding Shortfall Could Disrupt Learning in Schools
articles.desc: Secondary school principals warn that a capitation funding shortfall could disrupt learning as schools begin the third term
articles.content:
Secondary school principals have raised fresh concerns over government capitation, warning that continued funding shortfalls could disrupt learning as schools begin the third term.

The concerns were raised on Tuesday by the Kenya Secondary Schools Heads Association, whose chairperson Willie Kuria said many institutions were struggling to meet their financial obligations because they had not received the full annual capitation allocation per learner.

According to the principals, the government is expected to provide KSh22,244 annually for each learner. However, schools say the funds available to them remain below that amount, leaving administrators under pressure as they run academic programmes and meet essential expenses.

The funding concerns come only days after learners returned for the third term, a critical period for schools preparing candidates for national examinations.

School heads say inadequate funding affects their ability to pay for essential services and supplies, including food, water, electricity and other day-to-day operations.

The issue has also raised questions about the difference between funds announced as released by the government and the actual amount that reaches individual school accounts.

Kuria said some of the money is retained for specific education-related activities, meaning the amount available directly to school administrators can be lower than the figure publicly announced as released.

For parents and learners, the concern is whether the funding gap could eventually interfere with normal learning activities if schools continue struggling to meet operational costs.

The warning also places renewed attention on the wider challenge of financing public education at a time when the cost of food, utilities and other essential services has increased.

Education funding has remained a major concern for school administrators, particularly where institutions must continue operating even when capitation is delayed or falls below expected levels.

The principals are now calling for the government to address the shortfall and ensure schools receive adequate funding to run their programmes without disruption.

As the third term continues, attention will be on whether additional funds are released and whether the concerns raised by school heads can be resolved before the financial pressure affects learners more directly.

articles.title: Kenya Inflation Rises to 6.6% as Food and Transport Costs Climb
articles.desc: Kenya's inflation rose to 6.6% in August as higher food, transport and housing costs added pressure to household budgets.
articles.content:
Kenya's annual inflation rose to 6.6% in August 2026, adding fresh pressure to households as the cost of food, transport and other essential services continued to increase.

The latest figures from the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics show that inflation increased from 6.5% recorded in July.

Food and non-alcoholic beverages remained a major source of pressure, recording an annual increase of 9%. Transport costs also rose sharply, increasing by 15.7% over the year.

Housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuel-related costs increased by 3.6%, adding to the financial pressure facing households.

The figures help explain why many Kenyans continue to feel the impact of the rising cost of living even when some individual products become cheaper from one month to another.

During August, the prices of some household items declined, including sifted maize flour, tomatoes and diesel. However, increases in other goods and services continued to push overall consumer prices higher.

For households, higher transport costs can quickly affect daily spending, particularly for workers and families that rely on public transport. Rising food prices can also place additional pressure on monthly budgets.

Businesses are also affected when transport and operating costs increase. Companies involved in distribution and logistics may face higher expenses, while smaller businesses can struggle to absorb rising costs without increasing prices.

The August inflation figures also show how changes in fuel and transport costs can spread through the wider economy. When it becomes more expensive to move people and goods, businesses may face additional pressure across their supply chains.

Kenya's inflation remains within the Central Bank's target range, but the latest increase will still be closely watched because of its direct effect on household spending and business costs.

For ordinary consumers, the most important issue remains whether prices of essential goods and services will stabilise in the coming months.

The latest data puts renewed attention on the cost of living and the factors influencing how much Kenyan households spend on food, transport and basic services.

articles.title: CA Proposes New Safeguards for Recycling Inactive Mobile Numbers
articles.desc: The Communications Authority has proposed safeguards for inactive mobile numbers as Kenyans are invited to submit public views.
articles.content:
The Communications Authority of Kenya has opened public consultation on proposed safeguards that could change how inactive mobile phone numbers are deactivated and later recycled.

The draft procedures are intended to guide the handling of inactive telecommunication numbers while protecting the rights and interests of subscribers.

The Communications Authority says the framework is needed to help manage Kenya's numbering resources, which must remain available as demand for telecommunications services continues to grow.

The proposal is particularly important because mobile numbers have become closely connected to people's digital lives.

A phone number can be linked to mobile money, banking services, messaging platforms, social media accounts and other online services. Reassigning a number without proper safeguards could therefore create privacy and security concerns for a former subscriber.

The draft rules come after a High Court ruling that highlighted the importance of protecting mobile numbers as part of a person's digital identity.

The Communications Authority has invited members of the public and other stakeholders to submit their views before the proposed safeguards are finalised.

For ordinary mobile users, the consultation provides an opportunity to raise concerns about what should happen when a SIM card or mobile number becomes inactive.

The proposed framework is not simply about taking unused numbers out of circulation. It is also expected to establish clearer procedures for how numbers are handled before they are eventually made available to another user.

The issue matters because Kenya depends heavily on mobile communication and mobile-based financial services. A number that appears inactive may still have connections to important accounts or personal information.

Clear safeguards could therefore help reduce the risk of privacy breaches while allowing the country to manage its limited pool of mobile numbers more efficiently.

The Communications Authority has made the draft procedures available through its Open Consultations platform and is seeking public feedback before the final framework is adopted.

As the consultation continues, attention will focus on whether the proposed safeguards provide sufficient protection for subscribers while also meeting the growing demand for mobile numbering resources.

articles.title: JKIA Flights Resume After Aviation Workers Call Off Strike
articles.desc: JKIA operations are resuming after aviation workers called off their strike, with efforts underway to clear disrupted flights.
articles.content:
Flight operations at Jomo Kenyatta International Airport are beginning to return to normal after aviation workers called off a strike that disrupted travel and left passengers facing delays and cancellations.

The Kenya Aviation Workers Union ended the industrial action on Tuesday following talks with the government and aviation authorities.

Under a return-to-work agreement, affected workers were directed to resume their normal duties as efforts began to restore services and clear flights affected during the disruption.

The strike had caused significant problems at JKIA, Kenya's main international airport, with passengers experiencing long delays, cancellations and uncertainty over their travel plans.

For many travellers, the announcement that workers had returned to duty brings relief, but normal operations may take time to fully recover as airlines and airport authorities work through flights disrupted during the strike.

JKIA is one of East Africa's most important aviation hubs, meaning disruptions at the airport can affect not only Nairobi travellers but also regional and international connections.

The return to work is therefore expected to ease pressure on passengers, airlines and businesses that depend on reliable air transport.

The latest development follows days of disruption that left some travellers stranded and forced others to change their plans at short notice.

Passengers with upcoming flights are still advised to confirm their travel status directly with their airlines, particularly as schedules are adjusted while operations are restored.

The agreement ending the strike is also important because it shifts attention from the immediate disruption to whether the issues raised by aviation workers will now be addressed through the agreed process.

For Nairobi residents and travellers, the immediate focus remains the restoration of reliable airport services and the clearance of delayed flights.

As workers resume their duties, authorities will be under pressure to restore normal operations as quickly as possible and reduce further inconvenience for passengers.

articles.title: Rising Stars Draw South Sudan and Burundi in U-20 Qualifiers
articles.desc: Kenya's Rising Stars will face South Sudan and Burundi in Group C of the 2026 CECAFA U-20 AFCON qualifiers.
articles.content:
Kenya's Rising Stars will face South Sudan and Burundi after being drawn in Group C of the 2026 CECAFA U-20 AFCON qualifiers.

The draw was conducted on Monday, setting the stage for Kenya's latest attempt to secure a place at the continental youth championship.

The regional qualifiers are scheduled to take place in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, from September 15 to September 25.

Kenya will enter the competition hoping to build on its recent progress in youth football and secure another opportunity to compete at continental level.

Nine teams are expected to take part in the qualifiers, with the competition divided into three groups.

Under the tournament format, the winners of each group will qualify for the semi-finals alongside the best second-placed team across the three groups.

The two finalists will then earn qualification to represent the CECAFA region at the 2027 CAF U-20 Africa Cup of Nations in Ghana.

For the Rising Stars, the draw presents an early picture of the challenge ahead. Matches against South Sudan and Burundi will determine whether Kenya can progress from the group stage and move closer to continental qualification.

The campaign will also be an important test for the team's technical bench and emerging young players as Kenya continues to develop talent for future national teams.

Youth competitions play a major role in giving upcoming players international experience before they make the transition to senior football.

A strong performance in Tanzania could therefore benefit not only the current squad but also Kenya's wider football development plans.

Kenyan football fans will now turn their attention to preparations for the tournament and the final squad selected to represent the country.

With Group C now confirmed, the Rising Stars have a clear path ahead as they prepare to face South Sudan and Burundi in their bid for a place in the knockout stage.

articles.title: Emergency Jet Fuel Import Helps Avert Shortage at Kenya's Major Airports
articles.desc: Kenya brought in emergency jet fuel to prevent shortages at JKIA and Moi Airport as rising demand put supplies under pressure.
articles.content:
Kenya brought in an emergency shipment of jet fuel to prevent a potential shortage at Jomo Kenyatta International Airport and Moi International Airport as rising demand placed supplies under pressure.

The country received 30,000 tonnes of Jet A-1 fuel on August 20 outside the government's usual supply arrangement, according to a fresh report on the matter.

The emergency cargo was brought in after concerns emerged that available supplies might not meet demand during August.

Demand for jet fuel had increased sharply at Kenya's two major airports, particularly at JKIA, where increased international aviation activity contributed to higher fuel consumption.

The additional shipment was intended to bridge the anticipated supply gap and ensure airlines could continue operating without major disruption.

For travellers, a jet fuel shortage could have resulted in delayed or disrupted flights. Airlines depend on reliable fuel supplies to maintain schedules, while disruptions can affect passengers, tourism, cargo and business travel.

The situation also highlights the pressure that rising aviation activity can place on Kenya's fuel supply system.

According to the report, the emergency shipment was sourced outside the normal Government-to-Government fuel supply framework after logistical challenges made it difficult to bring forward a scheduled cargo.

The next shipment under the regular arrangement was expected in early September, leaving Kenya exposed to a possible supply gap had the emergency cargo not been secured.

The special import came at a higher cost than the normal supply arrangement, underlining the financial impact of responding to an unexpected demand increase.

For Kenya's aviation sector, maintaining reliable fuel supplies is essential because JKIA serves as the country's main international gateway, while Moi International Airport plays an important role in connecting the Coast to domestic and international markets.

The emergency shipment helped prevent an immediate shortage, but the development raises broader questions about how Kenya plans for sudden increases in aviation fuel demand.

As air travel and regional aviation activity continue to change, maintaining sufficient reserves will remain important for protecting flight operations and avoiding costly disruptions.

articles.title: Kenya Police Bullets Miss CAF Ticket After Extra-Time Final Defeat
articles.desc: Kenya Police Bullets lost 1-0 to Kawempe Muslim after extra time, missing out on the CAF Women's Champions League.
articles.content:
Kenya Police Bullets have missed out on a place in the CAF Women's Champions League after losing 1-0 to Uganda's Kawempe Muslim Ladies in the CECAFA qualifiers final in Kigali.

The tightly contested final remained goalless after 90 minutes, with neither side able to find the breakthrough during normal time.

The decisive moment came in the 100th minute of extra time when Kawempe captain Agnes Nabukenya scored from close range to put the Ugandan side ahead.

Kenya Police Bullets pushed for an equaliser but were unable to find a way back before the final whistle, ending their hopes of securing the region's ticket to the continental competition.

The defeat will be particularly painful for the Kenyan champions after a strong run through the regional qualifiers. Police Bullets reached the final following an impressive 5-0 victory over South Sudan's Yei Joint Stars in the semi-finals.

The campaign had given the team a real opportunity to compete among Africa's leading women's clubs, but the final proved to be one step too far.

For Kenyan women's football, the result is a reminder of how narrow the margins can be in regional competition. A single goal separated Police Bullets from continental qualification after a hard-fought 100 minutes of football.

The loss also means Kawempe Muslim Ladies will represent the CECAFA region at the 2026 CAF Women's Champions League.

Despite the disappointment, Kenya Police Bullets leave the qualifiers having demonstrated their ability to compete strongly against some of the region's leading women's teams.

Their journey to the final included a dominant semi-final performance and showed the growing strength of Kenya's domestic women's game.

Attention will now turn to the club's next campaign and whether the experience gained in Kigali can help Police Bullets make another push for continental qualification.

For supporters, the immediate feeling will be one of heartbreak. But reaching another major regional final also underlines that the Kenyan champions remain among the teams capable of challenging for bigger honours in the future.

articles.title: Kenya Railways Adds Special Trains as Aviation Disruptions Continue
articles.desc: Kenya Railways has added special Nairobi–Mombasa services, giving travellers more options as aviation disruptions continue.
articles.content:
Kenya Railways has introduced additional special train services between Nairobi and Mombasa, offering travellers more options as disruptions continue to affect the aviation sector.

The extra Madaraka Express services were announced on Monday and will operate over August 31 and September 1.

Kenya Railways said the additional trips are available for booking and encouraged passengers to reserve seats early.

The move comes as aviation disruptions have left many travellers facing delayed, cancelled or rescheduled flights. For passengers who still need to travel between Nairobi and Mombasa, the additional rail services provide another transport option during the disruption.

According to the announced schedule, a special train was set to depart Mombasa Terminus at 8:40pm on Monday. On Tuesday, additional services are scheduled from Nairobi Terminus at 9:40am and Mombasa Terminus at 4:30pm.

The development is particularly relevant to travellers whose plans have been affected by the ongoing disruption in airport operations.

For many passengers, transport disruptions can lead to missed connections, cancelled meetings and unexpected accommodation costs. The availability of extra train services could therefore help ease some of the pressure on travellers seeking to move between Kenya's capital and the Coast.

The announcement also highlights the importance of alternative transport networks when a major sector faces disruption.

Passengers planning to use the additional services have been advised to make bookings early because demand may increase as more travellers look for alternatives to air travel.

For now, the special services offer a practical option for people travelling along one of Kenya's busiest transport corridors while aviation operations remain under pressure

articles.title: KUCCPS Reopens KMTC Applications, Giving Students Another Chance
articles.desc: KUCCPS has reopened applications for selected KMTC programmes, giving eligible students another chance to join the September 2026 intake.
articles.content:
Students seeking to join the Kenya Medical Training College have received another opportunity after the Kenya Universities and Colleges Central Placement Service reopened applications for selected programmes ahead of the September 2026 intake.

The latest application window gives eligible candidates another chance to compete for available places, particularly those who missed an earlier opportunity or were unable to secure placement.

The reopening is significant for students hoping to pursue careers in Kenya's health sector, where KMTC remains one of the country's key training institutions for medical and health-related professionals.

For many young people and their families, missing an application deadline can delay education and career plans. A reopened window can therefore provide a fresh opportunity for candidates still seeking placement.

Reports published Monday indicate that selected diploma and certificate programmes are available under the latest application exercise, with applicants expected to use the KUCCPS student portal.

The opportunity also highlights the importance of students checking programme requirements carefully before submitting their choices. Different courses have different entry qualifications, meaning candidates should ensure their KCSE results meet the requirements for their preferred programmes.

Applicants should also confirm the availability of programmes and follow official KUCCPS instructions when submitting applications.

The development matters beyond the students applying today. Access to medical training helps prepare future health workers who may eventually serve communities across Kenya.

For families with students still searching for education opportunities, the reopened application window offers another pathway into professional training rather than waiting for a future intake.

The key message for eligible applicants is to act within the available application period and rely on official KUCCPS information when making their choices.

As the September 2026 intake approaches, the reopening gives students with an interest in medical and health-related careers another chance to secure a place in training.

articles.title: Milk Supply Pressure Raises Price Concerns as COFEK Calls for Action
articles.desc: Falling formal milk supplies have raised price concerns as COFEK gives the government seven days to outline urgent action.
articles.content:
Kenyans could face increased pressure on milk prices after formal-sector supplies declined, prompting the Consumers Federation of Kenya to demand urgent government action.

New data cited by COFEK shows that formal milk intake fell from 88.89 million litres in May to 84.44 million litres in June, a five per cent month-to-month decline.

The consumer body has now called on the government to outline measures within seven days to address supply challenges and protect consumers from further price increases.

The issue is already being felt in parts of the market. COFEK says some retailers in Nairobi have begun rationing purchases, while fresh milk prices at some outlets have increased.

For households, milk is an everyday commodity, meaning changes in supply and prices can quickly affect family budgets. The situation also affects retailers and dairy farmers who depend on a stable market.

Smallholder farmers, who provide a major share of Kenya's milk supply, are facing pressure from reduced pasture availability and rising animal-feed costs, according to COFEK.

The federation says some farmers have reported lower milk yields, adding to concerns about the stability of supply if the challenges continue.

COFEK has called for coordinated action involving the Ministry of Agriculture, the Kenya Dairy Board and the National Treasury. Its demands include a recovery plan, support to affected dairy farmers and closer monitoring of retail prices.

The development has also renewed attention on Kenya's ability to manage milk shortages after periods of surplus production.

For consumers, the key question is whether action can stabilise supply before shortages become more widespread and prices rise further.

The government's response in the coming days will therefore be closely watched by households, farmers and businesses across the dairy sector.

articles.title: Stolen Phone Leads Police to Suspected Nairobi Handset Network
articles.desc: A stolen phone led police to a Nairobi shop where 12 other handsets were recovered as investigations into a suspected network continue.
articles.content:
A stolen mobile phone has led police to a shop in Nairobi suspected of being linked to the illegal trade in stolen handsets, opening fresh investigations into a possible wider network.

Officers from Embakasi and Central police stations launched an undercover operation along Munyu Road after receiving information about the stolen device.

The operation led to the arrest of a suspect, who police say provided investigators with leads after questioning.

According to the National Police Service, the suspect allegedly said he had bought the phone from people known to him before selling it on.

A search at the premises later uncovered 12 additional mobile phones and six phone batteries, raising suspicion that the location may have been used to receive and trade in stolen devices.

Police are now pursuing other suspects identified during the operation as investigations continue into how the alleged network operates and how stolen phones move through the trade.

The case matters to Nairobi residents because mobile phone theft remains a daily concern in many parts of the city. For victims, losing a phone can mean more than losing an expensive device, particularly where personal information, mobile money services and important contacts are involved.

The latest operation also shifts attention to the market that may exist after a phone is stolen. Recovering suspected devices can help investigators trace possible links between those who steal phones and individuals accused of receiving or reselling them.

The National Police Service has urged members of the public to report suspicious activity to the nearest police station.

As investigations continue, police are expected to establish whether the Munyu Road operation was linked to a broader network dealing in stolen handsets.

For Nairobi residents, the outcome could provide important answers about how stolen phones are moved and sold within the city and whether those behind the alleged trade can be brought to account.

articles.title: Hundreds Remain Stranded at JKIA as Aviation Workers' Strike Continues
articles.desc: Hundreds of passengers remain stranded at JKIA as an aviation workers' strike enters its second day, disrupting flights and airport operations.
articles.content:
Hundreds of passengers remained stranded at Jomo Kenyatta International Airport on Monday as an aviation workers' strike continued to disrupt flights and airport operations.

Some travellers spent Sunday night at the airport after delays and uncertainty affected their travel plans. Others arrived on Monday hoping to board rescheduled flights but were still waiting for updates on when they would depart.

The disruption followed industrial action involving members of the Kenya Aviation Workers Union, whose grievances include concerns over welfare, working conditions and the implementation of previously agreed employment benefits.

The strike has affected aviation operations beyond Nairobi, but JKIA has become the centre of the disruption because of its role as Kenya's main international aviation hub.

For passengers, the impact has gone beyond delayed flights. Travellers have faced uncertainty over connections, accommodation and changes to plans that may have been arranged days or weeks earlier.

Some airlines have reportedly begun making arrangements for affected passengers, including hotel transfers in certain cases, as the disruption continues.

The situation also highlights the wider effect of industrial disputes at critical public facilities. A disruption at JKIA can quickly affect travellers, airlines, businesses and families, particularly when passengers are connecting to regional and international destinations.

Airport authorities have also advised passengers to confirm their flight status with their respective airlines before travelling, as delays continue to affect departures.

The immediate concern for travellers is when normal operations will resume and whether the dispute between workers and the affected aviation institutions can be resolved.

For those still waiting at JKIA, however, the most pressing issue remains clear: receiving reliable information about their flights and knowing when their journeys can continue.

As the strike enters its second day, attention will remain on negotiations and any agreement that could restore normal operations at Kenya's busiest airport.

articles.title: Kenya Boosts Power Imports as Rising Demand Puts Grid Under Pressure
articles.desc: Kenya increased electricity imports from Ethiopia and Uganda as rising demand put pressure on local generation and raised concerns over power rationing.
articles.content:
Kenya is increasingly relying on electricity imports from neighbouring countries as rising demand continues to put pressure on the national power grid.

New data for the six months to June 2026 shows that imported electricity accounted for 12 per cent of the power supplied to Kenya Power, up from 10 per cent during the same period last year. Ethiopia remained the main source of the additional imported supply, while imports from Uganda also increased.

The growing dependence highlights a challenge facing Kenya's energy sector: electricity demand from homes and businesses is rising faster than the available cushion in local generation capacity.

For ordinary consumers, the issue matters because a tight electricity reserve can increase the risk of supply interruptions, particularly during periods of high demand. Businesses can also face disruption when unreliable power affects operations, production and operating costs.

Kenya Power has previously warned that dependence on imported hydropower carries risks of its own. A serious drought or other disruption in neighbouring countries could affect their ability to maintain electricity exports to Kenya.

The pressure on the grid has also been reflected in concerns over the country's shrinking reserve margin. Recent reporting showed that the gap between available electricity capacity and demand had narrowed, increasing concerns about possible power cuts if supply comes under further strain.

Imported electricity is helping Kenya meet current demand, but the trend raises wider questions about long-term energy security.

A growing economy requires reliable electricity for households, factories, hospitals, schools and small businesses. While regional power trading can provide an important backup, Kenya's long-term stability will also depend on expanding and strengthening domestic generation.

The increase in imports therefore tells two sides of the same story.

On one hand, regional connections with countries such as Ethiopia and Uganda are helping Kenya keep electricity flowing when local supply is under pressure. On the other, the growing reliance exposes how narrow the country's electricity reserve has become.

For consumers, the most important question is whether Kenya can maintain reliable power while demand continues to rise.

The answer will depend on how quickly new local generation comes online and whether the country can strengthen its grid before supply pressure turns into more widespread electricity interruptions.

articles.title: Kenya Police Bullets Reach CECAFA Final After 5-0 Win Over Yei Joint Stars
articles.desc: Kenya Police Bullets thrashed Yei Joint Stars 5-0 in Kigali to reach the CECAFA qualifiers final and move closer to CAF Women's Champions League qualification.
articles.content:
Kenya Police Bullets have booked their place in the final of the CAF Women's Champions League CECAFA qualifiers after a commanding 5-0 victory over South Sudan's Yei Joint Stars in Kigali, Rwanda.

The Kenyan side produced a dominant performance in Saturday's semi-final at Kigali Pele Stadium, securing a place in the regional final and keeping their hopes of reaching the CAF Women's Champions League alive.

The result is a major step for Kenya Police Bullets, who have been among the leading sides in the regional competition and entered the knockout stage with confidence after their earlier performances.

Their emphatic semi-final victory now puts them one match away from securing the CECAFA zone's place at the continental tournament. The winner of the regional qualifiers earns the sole ticket to represent the zone at the CAF Women's Champions League final tournament.

Kenya Police Bullets will face Uganda's Kawempe Muslim Ladies in the final after the Ugandan side defeated Commercial Bank of Ethiopia 3-0 in the other semi-final on Saturday.

The final will therefore offer the Kenyan champions an opportunity to turn a strong regional campaign into continental qualification.

For Kenyan women's football, the result is also another positive moment for a domestic club competing beyond the country's borders. Success in regional competition gives Kenyan players greater exposure and provides a platform to test themselves against some of East and Central Africa's strongest teams.

The 5-0 scoreline underlines the authority with which Kenya Police Bullets handled the semi-final, but the biggest test is still ahead.

A place in the final guarantees nothing beyond Saturday's victory. The continental ticket will be decided by the outcome of the final, making the next match the most important of the campaign.

Kenya Police Bullets will now shift their attention to Kawempe Muslim Ladies as they seek to finish the qualifiers on a high and secure a place among Africa's leading women's clubs.

The victory gives Kenyan football supporters another positive result to celebrate tonight, while attention now turns to whether the Bullets can complete their regional campaign with the title.

articles.title: Youth Storm Utimo Sacco Offices Over Death of Man in Matatu Incident
articles.desc: Youth and community members stormed Utimo Sacco offices in Buruburu, demanding accountability over the death of Brian Wafula.
articles.content:
Youth and community members staged protests in Nairobi on Saturday after storming the offices of Utimo Matatu Sacco in Buruburu, demanding accountability over the death of Brian Wafula.

The protests followed an incident reported to have occurred about two weeks ago near Space Mall in Umoja. Wafula allegedly died after being pushed from a moving matatu following a dispute over payment.

According to accounts from his colleagues, Wafula had helped the matatu crew free their vehicle after it became stuck in mud. A disagreement later emerged over payment for the assistance.

Wafula reportedly boarded the vehicle while demanding the money he was owed. During the confrontation, he was allegedly pushed from the moving matatu and suffered serious head injuries.

His death has now triggered anger among colleagues and members of the community, leading to Saturday's protest at the Sacco offices.

Police were deployed as protesters blocked access to the offices and demanded answers over the incident.

The matter remains under investigation. Police in Buruburu said the matatu linked to the incident has been traced and impounded for examination, while efforts to locate the crew involved continue.

The case has drawn attention to accountability in public transport and the safety of passengers and other people who interact with matatus on Nairobi's busy roads.

For Wafula's family and colleagues, however, the immediate concern remains justice and the identification of those responsible for his death.

His body remains at the Mama Lucy Hospital morgue as the family prepares for his burial. Family members and colleagues have also appealed for support to help facilitate the funeral arrangements.

Saturday's protests add fresh pressure for progress in the investigation as the community awaits further action from police.

As investigations continue, the case is expected to remain under close watch, particularly over whether the matatu crew will be traced and held accountable if evidence establishes criminal responsibility.

articles.title: Kenyan YouTube Creators Face New 5% Tax Deduction on Earnings
articles.desc: Kenyan YouTube creators face a new 5% withholding tax on earnings as Google requires AdSense users to submit KRA PIN details.
articles.content:
Kenyan YouTube content creators are facing a new deduction on their earnings after Google notified eligible AdSense for YouTube users about a 5 per cent Kenyan withholding tax. 

The deduction is expected to first apply to September 2026 earnings, with affected creators beginning to see its impact when eligible payments are made in October. Google has also asked Kenyan creators to provide their Kenya Revenue Authority Personal Identification Numbers through AdSense for YouTube. 

For creators who depend on YouTube as a source of income, the change means that a portion of their earnings will now be withheld before they receive their final payments.

The development has triggered concern among some Kenyan creators, particularly those who use YouTube revenue to support themselves, employ production teams or reinvest earnings into cameras, internet, editing and other content-production costs.
Google says the requirement is linked to compliance with Kenya's tax laws. Creators using affected accounts have been asked to submit their KRA PIN information before the stated deadline.

The issue highlights the growing importance of Kenya's digital economy.

Content creation has increasingly become a source of income for young people and entrepreneurs, with creators earning through advertising, brand partnerships and other online opportunities.

As more digital platforms connect Kenyan users to international markets, questions around taxation, reporting and compliance are becoming more important.

For creators, the immediate concern will be understanding exactly how the deduction affects their earnings and ensuring that their tax information is correctly submitted.

The wider question is how Kenya can develop a tax system that supports compliance while recognising that many digital creators operate as small businesses with production and operating costs.

The new deduction is therefore more than a YouTube story. It reflects the changing reality of work and business in Kenya, where an increasing number of people earn their income online.

articles.title: Fertiliser Subsidy Programme Loses More Than 426,000 Kenyan Farmers
articles.desc: More than 426,000 farmers left Kenya's fertiliser subsidy programme in the year to June, raising fresh questions about access to farm inputs.
articles.content:
Kenya's subsidised fertiliser programme has recorded a sharp decline in the number of farmers accessing the scheme, with more than 425,000 farmers dropping out during the year ending June.

The decline is significant because the fertiliser subsidy programme is one of the government's key measures aimed at lowering farming costs and supporting food production across the country. 

Access to affordable fertiliser can directly influence how much farmers plant and ultimately harvest. When fewer farmers benefit from subsidised inputs, concerns can arise over whether the programme is reaching those who need it and whether production could be affected.

The development comes as the government continues to push measures intended to strengthen food security. President William Ruto recently announced plans to further reduce the price of a subsidised 50-kilogramme bag of fertiliser from KSh2,500 to KSh2,000, alongside a proposed 50 per cent subsidy on maize seeds.

The contrasting developments raise an important question: if fertiliser prices are being lowered further, why has participation in the subsidy programme fallen?

The answer could lie in several factors, including access to distribution points, registration challenges, changing farming conditions and whether farmers can obtain the inputs when they need them during planting seasons.

For farmers, timing is as important as price. Fertiliser that is affordable but unavailable when planting begins may offer little benefit to a farmer who has already missed the season.
The issue also matters to consumers.

Lower agricultural production can eventually affect food availability and prices, particularly for crops that form a major part of household consumption. Supporting farmers with affordable inputs is therefore closely connected to wider efforts to maintain stable food supplies.

The decline in programme participation now puts attention on how the fertiliser subsidy is being implemented and whether more farmers can be brought back into the system.

As Kenya prepares for future planting seasons, the effectiveness of the programme will be measured not only by the announced price of fertiliser, but also by whether farmers across the country can actually access it when they need it.

articles.title: Gikomba Market Takes Shape as Nairobi Redevelopment Moves Forward
articles.desc: Three new multi-storey blocks are taking shape at Gikomba as Nairobi's major market undergoes redevelopment aimed at improving trading and safety.
articles.content:
Gikomba Market is taking a major step toward a new look, with three multi-storey blocks now under construction as the redevelopment of one of Nairobi's busiest trading centres moves forward.

An update issued on Wednesday by Interior Principal Secretary Raymond Omollo said roofing and internal installation works are underway on the three blocks forming the first phase of the project. 

The first phase is expected to provide trading spaces for up to 7,000 traders, including a dedicated fish-processing area designed for about 300 traders. The planned facilities also include a day-care centre, kitchens, sanitation facilities, an ICT hub, youth centre, basement parking, waste collection points and an integrated fire station. 

The redevelopment is significant for Gikomba because the market has operated for years through densely packed informal structures.

That environment has created challenges for traders and shoppers while making it difficult for emergency services to respond when fires occur. Flooding has also been a recurring problem in the market and surrounding areas. 

The new design is intended to move traders into organised, numbered and ventilated spaces while improving movement through the market.

Fire safety is particularly important.

Gikomba has experienced repeated fires over the years, with some incidents destroying traders' stock and causing deaths. The inclusion of an integrated fire station in the new development is therefore expected to improve emergency response within the market.

The project is also connected to the wider effort to improve the Nairobi River corridor. Earlier clearance of informal structures along the river formed part of the process leading into the redevelopment. 

For thousands of traders, however, redevelopment is ultimately about more than buildings.

Gikomba is a major source of livelihoods, attracting traders and customers from Nairobi and other parts of the country. Any change to the way stalls are allocated, accessed and operated can therefore affect businesses well beyond the market itself.

The first phase now offers a clearer picture of what the transformed market could look like.

As construction continues, attention will turn to completion, allocation of the new trading spaces and how traders will transition into the modernised facility.

For Nairobi, the project represents an attempt to address some of the longstanding problems surrounding one of the city's most important trading hubs while creating a more organised environment for commerce.

articles.title: From Kitui to Malkia Strikers: Josephine Kataa's Rise Continues
articles.desc: Josephine Kataa's journey from Kitui to Malkia Strikers highlights the rise of a new generation of Kenyan volleyball talent.
articles.content:
Josephine Kataa is emerging as one of the new faces in Kenya's women's volleyball setup as the Malkia Strikers prepare for a major continental assignment on home soil.

The KCB Volleyball Club player is part of the national team preparing for the 2026 CAVB Women's African Nations Volleyball Championship, which Kenya will host from August 23 to September 5.

Kataa's inclusion reflects the changing composition of a team that has traditionally combined experienced international players with emerging talent.

Her route into the national setup has taken her from Kitui to the national training environment at Kasarani, a journey highlighted in a profile published today.

The defender has also built her reputation at club level. Kataa plays for KCB Volleyball Club, which has supplied several players to the current Malkia Strikers squad.

Her selection is not simply about being part of a large squad. Kataa was recognised as the Best Libero during the 2026 Kenya Cup, adding a notable individual achievement to her rise in Kenyan volleyball.

The national assignment now presents a much bigger test.

Malkia Strikers enter the continental championship as defending champions and will be attempting to retain their title in front of a home crowd. Kenya's last continental triumph came in 2023, when the team defeated Cameroon in the final in Yaoundé.

The tournament carries significance beyond the African title. It is also connected to qualification for the 2027 FIVB Women's World Championship and the pathway toward the 2028 Los Angeles Olympic Games.

For Kataa and the other newcomers, that creates an opportunity to establish themselves on one of the biggest stages in African volleyball.

The competition for places will be demanding. Kenya's squad contains experienced internationals alongside players making their way into the national setup, meaning every training session and eventual selection decision carries weight.

For a player who has progressed from Kitui to representing one of Kenya's most successful national teams, the coming championship offers another stage in that development.

Kataa's story also reflects a broader feature of Kenyan sport: talent emerging from local competition can eventually find its way onto the national stage.

With the African championship now approaching, attention will turn to how the new generation performs when Malkia Strikers begin their title defence at home.

articles.title: Kenya Targets 5,500MW Power Capacity in Major Energy Expansion
articles.desc: Kenya is targeting 5,500MW of power capacity as it expands nuclear, geothermal and hydropower projects to meet rising electricity demand.
articles.content:
Kenya is significantly expanding its long-term electricity ambitions, with the country's renewable-energy development pipeline now targeting 5,500 megawatts (MW) as demand for power grows alongside industrialisation.

The expanded target is more than three times the previous 1,500MW ambition and includes plans for 2,000MW of nuclear power, 700MW of hydropower and additional geothermal generation.

Kenya already generates about 93 per cent of its electricity from renewable sources, giving the country one of the stronger clean-energy profiles in Africa. The expanded pipeline is intended to strengthen that position while providing additional generation capacity for a growing economy.

The scale of the plan matters for businesses.

Reliable electricity is important for manufacturers, technology companies, farms, shops and other enterprises whose operations depend on a stable power supply. More generation capacity could help Kenya respond to rising demand as industrial and commercial activity expands.

But producing more electricity does not automatically mean consumers will receive cheaper power.

Experts point to other parts of Kenya's electricity system—including transmission losses, financing costs, power-purchase agreements and grid efficiency—as factors that influence what households and businesses ultimately pay.

That makes the expansion a broader infrastructure story rather than simply a question of how many megawatts Kenya can generate.

For households, the important measure will eventually be whether increased generation and improvements across the electricity system translate into more reliable and affordable power.

For businesses, the potential benefits extend beyond electricity availability. A more dependable power system can reduce disruptions and help companies plan production and investment with greater certainty.

KenGen, which produces about 60 per cent of Kenya's electricity, is central to the expansion. The company has said its enlarged development pipeline reflects changing energy priorities, investment opportunities and rising regional demand for clean power.

The energy expansion also includes nuclear power, marking a significant shift in the scale and diversity of Kenya's future generation plans.

The challenge now is moving from ambitious capacity targets to projects that can be financed, built and connected efficiently to the national grid.

For Kenya's economy, the significance of the plan will ultimately be measured not only in megawatts added, but in whether those  megawatts support business growth, industrialisation and dependable electricity for consumers.

articles.title: Kenya to Import 25 Million Bags of Maize Amid Looming Food Shortage
articles.desc: Kenya will import 25 million bags of maize to address an expected food deficit after poor harvests raise concerns over future supplies and prices.
articles.content:
Kenya will import 25 million 90-kilogram bags of maize to bridge an expected food deficit after drought and other climate-related challenges reduced production in major maize-growing areas.

Agriculture Cabinet Secretary Mutahi Kagwe said the government has already made arrangements for the imports and assured Kenyans that measures are being put in place to protect food supplies.

Kenya consumes approximately 75 million bags of maize each year, while the government expects a shortfall of nearly 25 million bags because of reduced harvests. The planned imports are intended to help maintain supplies and limit the risk of sharp price increases.

The announcement comes after difficult weather conditions affected production in several important maize-growing regions.

For households, maize availability matters directly because maize flour remains a major part of the Kenyan diet. A significant reduction in domestic supply can place pressure on the price of maize and unga, particularly if demand remains high while local stocks fall.

Farmers are also facing the effects of the poor season. Reduced yields can mean lower incomes and less money available for the seeds, fertiliser and other inputs needed for the following planting season.

The government says maize imports will provide an immediate response while longer-term measures are pursued to strengthen domestic production.

Among those measures is the expansion of irrigation, including projects such as Galana Kulalu, aimed at reducing the country's dependence on rainfall and improving agricultural resilience. The government also plans to work with the National Treasury on tax and regulatory issues affecting farmers and agribusinesses.

The latest announcement marks a significant change from the one-million-bag import plan reported earlier this month, reflecting the scale of the food-supply concern now being presented by the government.

The immediate question for consumers will be whether the planned imports can arrive early enough to prevent shortages and contain pressure on maize prices.

For farmers, the bigger issue is whether the longer-term interventions can reduce Kenya's exposure to weather shocks and strengthen local production.

The government now faces the task of turning the import plan into actual supplies while working to ensure that Kenya's next harvest is stronger.

articles.title: EPRA Cuts Diesel Price by KSh5 as New Fuel Rates Take Effect
articles.desc: EPRA has cut diesel by KSh5 per litre, while petrol and kerosene prices remain unchanged under new fuel rates taking effect across Kenya
articles.content:
Kenyan motorists and businesses using diesel will get some relief at the pump after the Energy and Petroleum Regulatory Authority (EPRA) reduced the fuel’s maximum price by KSh5 per litre for the latest pricing cycle.

The new EPRA fuel prices took effect on August 15, 2026, and will remain in force until September 14. In Nairobi, diesel now has a maximum price of KSh217.86 per litre, down from KSh222.86. Super Petrol remains at KSh214.03, while kerosene stays at KSh191.38 per litre.

The reduction in diesel follows a decline in its average landed cost. EPRA reported that the cost fell by 13.08 per cent, from US$984.37 to US$855.59 per cubic metre between June and July.

Petrol and kerosene, meanwhile, would have faced upward pressure without government intervention. EPRA said KSh938 million in stabilisation support was used to keep their prices unchanged for the current cycle.

The diesel cut matters well beyond fuel stations.

Diesel is widely used by public transport operators, freight companies, farmers, manufacturers and other businesses. Lower fuel costs could reduce some operating expenses for enterprises that depend heavily on diesel, although the actual effect will vary from one business to another.

Transport fares will also be closely watched. A lower diesel price could ease pressure on operators, but it does not automatically mean passengers will pay less, since fares are affected by several other operating costs.

The cost of moving goods is another area to watch. Fuel forms part of the expense involved in transporting agricultural produce, manufactured goods and other products to markets. If lower diesel prices are sustained, businesses could potentially see some relief in distribution costs.

For households, the immediate change is narrower: diesel has fallen, while petrol and kerosene remain unchanged.

The new rates will run for one month before EPRA conducts its next scheduled review, leaving international oil prices and import costs among the factors to watch in the next pricing cycle.

For now, the KSh5 diesel reduction provides targeted relief to fuel users while leaving the prices of the other two regulated petroleum products unchanged.

articles.title: Nairobi Weather: Cool and Cloudy Conditions Expected This Week
articles.desc: Nairobi is expected to experience intermittent cool and cloudy conditions as Kenya Met forecasts generally dry weather across most of the country.
articles.content:
Nairobi residents can expect intermittent cool and cloudy conditions in the coming days as the Kenya Meteorological Department forecasts generally dry weather across most of Kenya.

The latest seven-day outlook, covering August 13 to 20, places Nairobi among several counties that could experience periods of cloud cover and cooler weather during the forecast period.

The forecast does not place Nairobi among the eight counties specifically highlighted as likely to receive rainfall during the period. Those counties include Bungoma, Trans Nzoia, Nakuru, Uasin Gishu, Elgeyo Marakwet, Kericho, Nyandarua and Nyeri.

For Nairobi residents, the forecast points to weather that may remain noticeably cool and cloudy at intervals rather than a prolonged spell of heavy rain.

That distinction matters for people planning their daily routines.

Commuters, outdoor traders, schools, construction workers and people travelling across the city can use the forecast to prepare for changing conditions, particularly during cooler or overcast periods.

The wider national picture remains relatively dry. Kenya Met expects most parts of the country to experience generally dry conditions, although some areas will continue to receive rainfall.

Nairobi's weather can also change within relatively short periods, meaning residents should not interpret the forecast as a guarantee that every part of the city will experience identical conditions.

The forecast is therefore most useful as a planning guide.

For anyone heading out early, cooler conditions may make warm clothing useful, while motorists and pedestrians should continue paying attention to local conditions where cloud cover or rain develops.

The weather outlook also comes as Kenya continues through the traditionally cool August period, with the Meteorological Department monitoring changing conditions across the country.

For Nairobi, the immediate forecast is less about heavy rainfall and more about cool, cloudy intervals amid generally dry conditions.

Residents should continue monitoring official weather updates as conditions can change and new forecasts are issued.

articles.title: Parklands Demolition Claims Clarified as Nairobi River Work Continues
articles.desc: Nairobi authorities have clarified viral claims about Parklands demolitions as the city continues its programme to restore riparian land along the river.
articles.content:
Viral claims of imminent demolitions in Parklands have prompted clarification from the Nairobi Rivers Commission and the Parks and Recreational Authority as work to reclaim riparian land along Nairobi’s rivers continues.

The clarification follows concerns among residents after information circulated about possible demolitions along the Kibagare River corridor. Officials said residents seeking information about notices, demarcation or verification should use official government channels rather than rely on unverified claims circulating online.

The issue matters because Nairobi’s river restoration programme is increasingly affecting areas where homes, businesses and other developments have been established close to river corridors.

The Nairobi Rivers Commission’s demarcation exercise covers about 27 kilometres, from Gitwamba Bridge to Naivasha Road, with the riparian boundary measured using a 30-metre buffer from the highest water mark, according to the Commission.

For Parklands residents and property owners, the distinction between an official notice, a demarcation exercise and an actual demolition order is important.

Unverified information can quickly create uncertainty for households and businesses, particularly where property ownership, development approvals and environmental regulations intersect.

The wider Nairobi River restoration programme is aimed at reclaiming riparian areas and improving the condition of the city's waterways. The government has been pursuing the programme through a multi-agency approach, with authorities identifying developments considered to be occupying protected river corridors.

That process, however, places a responsibility on authorities to communicate clearly with affected communities.

For residents, knowing whether a property has actually been identified for enforcement action is different from hearing that demolitions are about to take place.

The latest clarification therefore shifts attention back to official verification.
Residents with concerns over specific properties or notices have been urged to seek clarification through the relevant government offices rather than depend on social-media claims.

As Nairobi's river restoration programme continues, the balance between environmental protection, public safety and property interests is likely to remain an important issue for communities located along the city's waterways.

For Parklands, the immediate message is clear: verify before reacting, and seek official information where property or demolition claims are involved.

articles.title: From Lima to the estate, Kenya’s U20 stars and the fight for the future
articles.desc: Kenya finished second overall at the World U20 Championships in Lima, led by Franklin Kibet and a new wave of runners.
articles.content:
In Lima, under a sun that does not negotiate, Kenya’s young runners did what Kenya expects them to do: they ran, they suffered, and they brought medals home.

At the World U20 Championships, Kenya finished second overall in the medal standings, behind only the traditional athletics giants. Franklin Kibet led the charge, announcing himself on day one with gold, as the team collected three medals on the opening day and kept the pressure on through the final. By the time the closing ceremony arrived, Kenya had cemented its place as the top African nation at the global youth stage.

On the surface, this is familiar territory. Kenya at the top of the medal table, or close to it, is not news. But this team is different. These are not the same names we have chanted for a decade. These are new legs, new lungs, new stories. And that is where this story stops being just about sport and starts being about a country at a crossroads.

Why does this matter?
Because for years, Kenyan athletics has lived off the glory of its past. The same household names, the same marathons, the same records. Meanwhile, the pipeline—the U20s, the U18s, the county championships—was treated as a waiting room, not a battlefield. Lima changes that conversation. These athletes are not waiting their turn. They are demanding it.

For the parents watching in Kapsabet, Eldoret, Kiberia, and beyond, this is validation. The 4am runs in the dark. The borrowed shoes. The maize flour and beans diet. The sacrifices that no one sees until the flag goes up on a podium halfway across the world. This is proof that the grind still works.

But there is another side to this story, one that Kenya does not like to talk about.
Pressure.
